captions: Part three. Metrics and tools.
Where the model stops doing math, and starts
choosing.
Why define metrics in code? Look at this
2026 benchmark from dbt Labs.
When Claude Sonnet four point six wrote raw
SQL, it scored ninety percent. Through a semantic
layer, ninety eight point two.
For GPT five point three codex, eighty four
point one, versus one hundred.
The failure style matters even more. Raw SQL
fails silently, with a plausible wrong number. The
semantic layer fails loudly, with an error.
For numbers investors act on, loud failure is
what you want.
Here's a small semantic layer.
Revenue and PAT come straight from the facts
table.
Net margin is PAT over revenue. Debt to
equity is borrowings over equity. The model picks
net margin by name. It never writes the
formula itself.
Year on year compares a quarter with the
same quarter a year back, so it lags
by four.
Defaults live here too. Consolidated basis, and the
Indian fiscal year, April to March. So Q1
FY26 means April to June twenty twenty five.
And sanity checks. A net margin above a
hundred percent is not a great quarter. It's
a unit error.
Here's what one tool call returns. Eight quarters
for Acme.
Revenue and PAT come from the PDFs. The
violet columns are computed by the semantic layer:
net margin, and revenue growth year on year.
The same quarter a year ago had a
margin of 7.32 percent.
Now it's 8.50 percent.
That's the first half of our answer, and
nobody did the arithmetic in their head.
Now the tools. Keep them few and high
level.
List sources tells the agent what data exists
and how fresh it is.
Get metrics is the workhorse, the semantic layer.
Query SQL is for exploration, read-only and capped
at fifty rows.
Search docs finds commentary and returns document and
page.
Read table opens the exact table behind any
fact, for audits.
And run python is a sandbox for custom
transforms, like a trailing twelve month sum.
Two more, recall and remember, handle memory. We'll
get to those.
Tool design matters as much as the model.
Anthropic's guidance on writing tools boils down to
a few rules.
The description says when to use the tool,
not only what it does. Here it says:
prefer this over raw SQL.
Errors should teach. Ask for net profit, and
the error says: unknown metric, did you mean
PAT? The model fixes itself on the very
next step.
And outputs stay compact. Clip the rows, and
always return provenance.
